body: Credit: Oliver Cragg / Android Authority TL;DR The Hokkaido emulator for running Switch 2 games on Android now has built-in Banana Native support. This means you can generate and play native ports of Switch 2 titles via the emulator. Switch 2 emulation and ports require an Android device with high-end silicon and plenty of RAM, though. The Nintendo Switch 2 only launched last year, but we’ve recently seen the first emulators arriving on Android, along with native game ports. The port is generated entirely within the emulator’s UI.

title: Google Voice on Android gets redesign, hints at future RCS support

body: TL;DR Google is rolling out a redesign of the Google Voice app on Android. The new look borrows heavily from Google Messages, including a rounded text field and an “SMS” label on the send button. The redesign also hints that RCS support could be coming to Google Voice soon. Google Voice has been getting some much-needed attention lately. We recently found evidence of RCS support in an app teardown, and shortly after, we saw a redesign appear in its web app interface . That redesign also showed new service indicators — SMS or MMS — which could be in preparation for RCS support. Now, that redesign is rolling out to the Google Voice Android app as well, as spotted by 9to5Google . The redesign is reportedly rolling out in the latest version of the Google Voice app (v019342246) and looks clearly inspired by Google Messages. There’s a rounded text field at the bottom with attachment and camera icons. There’s also a new long-press gesture that opens up a context menu, similar to Google Messages.

title: YouTube’s new ‘co-view’ count for TV estimates the number of people watching TV at once
summary: By guessing the total number of viewers in front of the TV.
body: Credit: Ryan Haines / Android Authority TL;DR YouTube will now start showing a new “co-view” count on all videos watched on TV. This new metric accounts for multiple people watching on the same set at the same time, for both long-form videos and Shorts. It says the new metrics will help creators gauge their true reach on TV. YouTube is taking a page out of digital broadcasters ‘ playbook and adding a new view metric that will be publicly available. This new metric is called “co-view,” and it estimates the total number of people who watched a particular video while accounting for multiple people watching on a single TV set. With this, both Shorts and long-form videos will now display the number of co-views alongside a regular view count . Co-views are exclusive to YouTube’s TV app and won’t appear on mobile or desktop. Co-view data will be available starting today, and won’t apply to older views. However, it will apply to all existing and new videos on the platform.

If you’ve ever wondered what Android was like before gesture navigation, expandable notifications, or even an on-screen back button, a new website could scratch that itch. body: TL;DR Google has released v26.45 of Google Play Services. It lets your Wear OS watch use your phone’s GNSS to track location during outdoor workouts, which helps conserve watch battery life. The Play Store v54.1 also adds the Pixel virtual gamepad for compatible games when your Pixel Fold is open. If you often use your Wear OS smartwatch to track outdoor workouts, you may be aware of the impact it can have on battery life. Google is now rolling out a new feature that should help. Google has released a new version of Google Play Services (v26.45) that adds a feature letting your watch use your phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) to track your location during outdoor workouts. GNSS is a term for satellite-based positioning systems, such as GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, and NavIC. Running the watch’s GNSS receiver for an entire workout uses a lot of battery. By offloading that job to your smartphone, Google wants to make your watch’s battery last longer. Fitbit already offers something similar on some of its trackers with its Dynamic GPS feature.

title: US cities have some of the world’s weakest indoor mobile signals, Ookla finds
summary: Better indoor reception starts with better outdoor coverage.
body: TL;DR A new Ookla study ranks North America among the worst-performing regions globally for indoor 4G signal strength. Weak indoor signals affect 41% of measured buildings in Miami, 38% in Los Angeles, and 25% in New York, compared to just 2% in Seoul. Weak outdoor coverage explains about 85% of the differences in indoor signal strength between cities, although dedicated in-building cellular equipment can significantly improve reception. Much has been made of the strides US carriers have made in improving their networks, with recent reports highlighting everything from faster download speeds to wider 5G coverage . But those improvements may not mean much when you’re struggling to upload a photo from your living room. New research suggests American cities have some catching up to do when it comes to delivering reliable mobile coverage inside buildings.
